text: For three thousand years, the peoples of Mesoamerica, from central Mexico to Honduras, shared one religion.
The Pyramid of the Sun at the city of Teotihuacan was finished more than 1,800 years ago.
src: For three thousand years the peoples of Mesoamerica, from the Olmecs to the Maya and the Aztecs, shared a religion / the region stretching from central Mexico to Honduras and El Salvador
its Pyramid of the Sun, completed around 200 CE

text: They believed in many gods, like Tlaloc, the rain god, who lived in mountains and brought rain for the maize.
In their stories, the gods gave their own lives to set the sun moving.
src: the rain and storm god, called Tlaloc by the Aztecs and Chaak by the Maya, who lived in mountains and brought the rain on which maize depended
the other gods sacrificed themselves to set it moving

text: In pyramid temples, kings and priests offered the gods incense, their own blood, and sometimes human lives.
Time was sacred, and a calendar of 260 days guided the fate of each person.
src: Kings and priests offered the gods incense, their own blood and, at times, human lives in pyramid temples
A ritual calendar of 260 days, made of twenty named days combined with the numbers one to thirteen, governed divination and the fate of every person born on a given day

text: By their tradition, the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan where their god promised they would see an eagle on a cactus.
When the Spanish conquered the land, their missionaries destroyed temples, images and books.
src: by their tradition, founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, where their god Huitzilopochtli had promised they would see an eagle on a cactus
The Spanish conquest brought the destruction of the public religion / destroyed temples, images and books

text: Priests had kept painted books of bark paper or deerskin, folded like screens.
Only a few survive, such as four Maya books, kept today in Dresden, Madrid, Paris and Mexico City.
src: on long strips of bark paper or deerskin, coated with lime and folded like screens, which were kept by priests
only four Maya books survive today, in Dresden, Madrid, Paris and Mexico City

text: The Popol Vuh, a Maya book written down after the conquest, tells how the gods made people from maize.
Today, Maya day-keepers in Guatemala still count the 260-day calendar.
src: The greatest surviving work of Maya religious literature is the Popol Vuh / written in the K’iche' language in Latin letters by K’iche' nobles in the mid-16th century / the making of humans from maize
In the highlands of Guatemala, Maya day-keepers still count the 260-day calendar
